AMD Stock Dropped 11% Last Week. Is Intel's PC Warning Really That Bad? ©@undefined from Getty Images Pro via Canva, @Kittipong Jirasukhanont from PhonlamaiPhoto's Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) stock declined approximately 11% from October 30 to November 6, closing near $449 as semiconductor valuations came under pressure.

Intel (INTC) warned that PC weakness could extend into 2027, while AMD's third-quarter data center revenue surged 97% to $8.5 billion.

AMD expects approximately $17 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, but its premium valuation leaves limited room for weaker earnings growth.

What Happened?

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) stock dropped approximately 11% from October 30 to November 6, closing near $449 as investors weighed weakening PC demand against AMD's accelerating AI infrastructure growth.

Intel's October 29 earnings report added to concerns about semiconductor demand, with fourth-quarter revenue guidance of $15 billion to $16 billion and a warning that PC weakness could continue into 2027.

Intel CFO David Zinsner said, "we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," highlighting continued uncertainty across consumer computing markets.

However, AMD's November 3 earnings report presented a stronger picture of semiconductor demand.

The company reported third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45% year over year, while adjusted earnings per share climbed 74% to $2.09.

Data center revenue surged 97% to $8.5 billion, driven by strong demand for AMD Instinct GPUs and EPYC server processors.

AMD also projected approximately $17 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, representing 66% annual growth at the midpoint.

Despite those results, shares remained volatile, falling 17% on November 5 before rebounding 11% on November 6 as investors reassessed semiconductor valuations.

Intel's PC Warning Is a Smaller Problem for AMD

Intel's warning remains relevant because AMD still has meaningful exposure to consumer and commercial PC markets.

AMD's third-quarter client revenue increased 7% to $2.9 billion, although its broader Client and Gaming segment declined 8% to $3.7 billion.

However, data center revenue represented approximately 64% of AMD's quarterly sales, making AI infrastructure considerably more important to its overall growth.

Intel's data center and AI revenue increased 78% to $7.3 billion, demonstrating continued enterprise demand for server processors despite weaker PC conditions.

Intel also acknowledged supply constraints affecting its ability to meet strong Xeon demand, potentially creating opportunities for AMD to expand its EPYC server business.

AMD's growing AI partnerships, including Helios rack-scale systems installed and undergoing testing at Meta, further support its long-term growth prospects.

title: What Intel Doubters Got Wrong
detail:
What Intel Doubters Got Wrong
Bailey Pemberton
Sun, November 8, 2026 at 9:08 AM CST 4 min read
INTC
Trade Intel on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

If you had been weighing Intel in early November 2025, the headlines were already split between a complex restructuring plan and questions about whether AI-focused partnerships could offset organizational drag. Holding Intel over the past year would have returned 47.6%, including dividends. If you were setting up a position on 2025-11-06, the real puzzle was how to balance hopes around AI and foundry deals with concerns about bureaucracy, execution and future profitability.

The move put Intel in the middle of this trade. Scan 53 AI infrastructure stocks for other companies exposed to it.

The Two Intel Stories Investors Were Arguing About

The shares cost US$37.24 at the start of the period, and anyone looking at Intel then had to choose between a confident product revival story and a slower, restructuring heavy reset.

The bullish roadmap described a fair value of US$79, which reflected expectations of 10.0% revenue growth and a 22.0% profit margin over five years as new PC and data center chips rolled out.

The cautious restructuring view indicated a fair value of US$25.18, based on revenue rising 3.5% a year and profit margins reaching 7.8% while AI partnerships and foundry efforts were established.

NasdaqGS:INTC 1-Year Stock Price Chart
What The Results Changed For The Intel Thesis

Intel's later quarters brought heavy AI contracts and partnerships, yet the cleanest test of the original debate came from the Q3 2026 figures. Revenue reached US$16,513m versus US$13,653m a year earlier, but net income slipped to US$3,320m and net margin moved from 29.8% to 20.1%. That mix of higher sales and weaker profitability cut both ways for the bullish and cautious cases.

The whole episode turned on one assumption that applies well beyond Intel. Hopes around product revivals and AI exposure still needed margins to hold up. When you assess another chip stock, do not just track headline demand or revenue. Watch whether net margin and absolute profit move in the same direction as the growth story being sold.

What Intel's Recent Run Already Prices In

Intel trades at US$56.28 today after a 47.6% gain over the past year, and the selected Narrative's Fair Value sits below that quote. The Narrative leans on Intel's scale in PCs, servers and AI chips while questioning how far the turnaround can carry manufacturing and product credibility.

The key question now is what must keep going right for that higher price to hold, and the Narrative points squarely at one hurdle a buyer needs to judge: that Intel's push to compress several new process nodes into a short window does not repeat past execution problems while rivals defend their lead.

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC), Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM), and Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL) all set record closes in June. Five months later, each stock is worth less than half as much.

Intel closed at $58.27 on Nov. 4, off around 59% from $140.94, its record close on June 22. Arm ended that day at $191.80, around 56% under its June 18 record close, and Marvell finished at $159.80, about 50% below where it closed on June 4.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

All three fell between around 4% and 7% on Nov. 4 alone, then slid further on Nov. 5. Investors were weighing whether Democrats' midterm wins might slow the build-out of artificial intelligence data centers, especially after Texas elected a governor who campaigned for a moratorium on new ones.

Falls this steep can make all three look like bargains. But each stock is still up over 40% in 2026. And only one of them expects its sales growth to keep speeding up, even as its stock got cheaper.

Marvell is that one, and it's the only one of the three I'd buy right now.

Image source: Getty Images.

Intel's PC problem

Intel's third quarter was strong, with revenue up 21% year over year. The problem is the outlook it gave on Oct. 29. Intel sees non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings of $0.25 per share for the fourth quarter, under half the $0.52 it earned in the third quarter.

PCs are the biggest reason. Higher memory prices have pushed up what new PCs cost, and Intel expects revenue in its PC chip segment to drop over 20% from the third quarter. Its chief financial officer, David Zinsner, sees the weakness lasting until at least mid-2027.

Yes, demand for Intel's server chips still tops what it can supply. But at around $54, Intel stock trades at around 36 times the earnings expected for 2026 and about 30 times the earnings expected for 2027.

Is Arm's royalty slowdown priced in?

Arm reported its fiscal 2027 second quarter (the three months ended Sept. 30) on the evening of Nov. 4. Revenue climbed 27% year over year to $1.44 billion, and its adjusted earnings per share increased 33% to $0.52.

The figure I'd follow most closely, though, is royalty revenue (the fees Arm gets for every Arm-based chip its partners ship). Royalties grew just 8% from a year earlier to $670 million, a sharp slowdown from 22% growth in fiscal Q1. Arm said memory prices hit the smartphone market and offset some of its gains elsewhere.

Key Takeaways

Broadcom fell 15.5% in the week to Nov. 5 as Intel's weak outlook and fears of tighter AI rules hit chip stocks, Nvidia and AMD included.

Broadcom put out no news, and analysts still expect its normalized EPS to more than quadruple by fiscal 2028.

The bigger risk is Broadcom's own: it backstops up to about $72 billion of financing for AI racks leased to Anthropic.

The stock trades well below its usual forward P/E, and its December report is the next test.

Broadcom (AVGO:NASDAQ) fell 15.5% in the week to Nov. 5 with no news of its own. Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) started a chip rout with a weak outlook, and fears of tighter AI rules after the midterms deepened it, dragging down Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) too.

Intel lit the fuse

Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion after the Oct. 29 close, short of the roughly $17 billion analysts expected. Broadcom lost 5.5% on Oct. 30, while Intel fell 28.6% and went on to lose 43.2% in the week to Nov. 5.

Democrats then won both chambers of Congress on Nov. 3. Chip stocks slid on Nov. 4, then plunged on Nov. 5 on worries about slower data center building, with Broadcom down 10.4% that day.

Nvidia fell 15.0% in the week, about as much as Broadcom. AMD lost 28.6%, even though its forecast after the Nov. 3 close called for about $17 billion of fourth-quarter revenue, above the roughly $16.2 billion analysts expected.

Nothing changed at Broadcom

In its fiscal third quarter, revenue rose 86% to $29.6 billion, and AI chip revenue jumped 221% to $16.7 billion. Committed contract value hit $179.2 billion at Aug. 2, and management is aiming for about $115 billion of AI revenue in fiscal 2027.

Power was already the bottleneck: CEO Hock Tan called land, power and the building shell "more than a big concern" on the third-quarter call. Tighter rules could make that worse, but the orders are already on the books.

Analysts expect normalized EPS of $11.67 for the fiscal year that ended Nov. 1, up about 70% from $6.82 in fiscal 2025, and $30.37 by fiscal 2028:

title: AI Stocks Are Falling; Bitcoin Is Holding Ground. Here's What Could Come Next.
detail:
AI Stocks Are Falling; Bitcoin Is Holding Ground. Here's What Could Come Next.
Alex Carchidi, The Motley Fool

It's been said that bull markets end when good news fails to boost prices, and that bear markets end when bad news fails to send prices lower. On that note, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) is 33.7% above its bear market lows in late June. Most of the high-flying artificial intelligence (AI) value-chain stocks, on the other hand -- including Intel, Oracle, Micron Technology, and Sandisk -- are down by between 20% and 62% in the same period.

There are plenty of good reasons for those stocks to be down. Yet aside from emerging factors like questionable future demand for some of the technologies those companies make, all of those players, as well as Bitcoin, have faced a constant onslaught of geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty this year. Their diverging prices amid those shared headwinds mean that one thing in particular could be coming next.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Bitcoin's floor hasn't collapsed yet

Bitcoin didn't just start shrugging off bad news in the last couple of months. On Sept. 15, the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act, a bill intended to set rules for crypto market structures. It briefly fell below $75,000 that day, then recovered within weeks.

Then, October saw the Nasdaq Composite index fall more than 5%, as big spenders on AI failed to wow the market with their earnings reports as well as their future projections. Bitcoin dropped 10.3% in the 30-day period ending on Nov. 5, but it largely traded in a range: every daily close was between $76,198 and $84,082, regardless of what was happening in the world. That resilience had to face down a handful of problems that also weighed on tech stocks.

For instance, on Oct. 28, the Federal Reserve voted to hold interest rates steady, and the very next day's hot inflation data caused markets to expect a December hike. Rate hikes tend to be bad for risky assets like AI stocks and cryptocurrencies, as higher rates mean investors can earn a better return on low-risk Treasuries.

Before that, Brent crude oil prices climbed in October as the prospect of continued war with Iran contributed to a highly uncertain environment. Uncertainty tends to weigh on riskier assets, and rising energy costs drive inflation, which might prompt the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates further.

Qualcomm (QCOM) stock gained 5.5% on Friday, November 6, 2026, while the S&P 500 rose 0.3%. The company issued no announcements, earnings reports or filings that day, and four of its five peers also finished higher. Separately, Reuters reported on Friday that Alphabet disclosed a Qualcomm stake worth $548 million. Friday's gain followed a 9.5% fall on Thursday, November 5, the day after Qualcomm reported its fiscal fourth-quarter results. So what changed for chip stocks, and for Qualcomm, between Thursday and Friday?

Qualcomm Rose As Chip Stocks Recovered From A Sell-Off

Qualcomm climbed on Friday as semiconductor shares bounced back from a sell-off. A Democratic sweep of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections raised fears in the market of a slowdown in data center spending, and stocks sold off sharply on Thursday. Chip stocks were lower across the board that day. Qualcomm led the decline after its fourth-quarter results slightly beat estimates but came with light guidance. Stocks recovered some of those losses on Friday, with Nvidia, AMD and other chip manufacturers rebounding alongside Qualcomm.

A partial recovery isn't an all-clear. But a year after 21 sell-offs this sharp, the S&P 500 was higher 20 times.

These market fears reach Qualcomm because the company is building a data center business alongside its phone chips. On its November 4 call, management reiterated its $5 billion revenue target for data center in fiscal 2027. Management said most of that revenue is custom silicon for AI accelerators at two large cloud customers.

How Did Qualcomm Compare With Other Chip Makers?

Qualcomm rose more than three of the five chip makers on its peer list. Texas Instruments was the only company among the five to fall. Advanced Micro Devices posted the largest rise in the group, gaining 11.0%, while Intel also rose more than Qualcomm.

The wider technology sector advanced at a slower pace. XLK, the SPDR fund that tracks the sector, gained 1.5%, finishing well short of Qualcomm's rise. Qualcomm moved in step with its chip peers rather than on its own.

Qualcomm Stock Is Still Down Over Twelve Months

A rise of this size is not rare for Qualcomm. The stock recorded 11 sessions with a gain at least this large in the prior 365 days, and its most recent move of this magnitude in either direction was Thursday's fall.

Friday's gain still left the stock down 6.0% over twelve months, while the S&P 500 returned 9.8%. Over the past six months alone, Qualcomm lost 23.8%, while the S&P 500 gained 0.25%. At $165.41, the stock closed about a third below its highest close of the past twelve months, $251.02 on May 29, 2026. It remains well above its lowest close of the year, $124.07 on April 7, 2026.

title: Here's Where I Think Intel Stock Will Be at the End of 2030
detail:
Here's Where I Think Intel Stock Will Be at the End of 2030
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool

INTC
NVDA

Trading disclosure

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) stock has given back a huge part of its 2026 gains. Shares ended at $60.55 on Nov. 3, around 57% under the $140.94 they ended at on June 22. The stock dropped 45% in October alone.

My estimate for $5,000 put into Intel stock at that price is around $5,400 when 2030 ends. That'd be a gain of less than 10% in a bit more than four years, or under 2% a year.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

What surprised me is that this number assumes Intel's business does well. My estimate has Intel more than doubling its earnings per share from this year to 2030.

Most of what keeps the result down is how much investors pay for Intel's earnings today.

Image source: Intel.

Intel's profits have bounced back fast

Showing how quickly the business has turned, Intel's non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share grew from $0.29 in the first quarter of 2026 to $0.42 in the second quarter and $0.52 in the third. A year before, in the third quarter of 2025, it was just $0.23. If Intel meets its fourth-quarter forecast of $0.25, its adjusted earnings per share for all of 2026 would total around $1.48 -- more than triple the $0.42 it made in 2025.

Intel's server chips are doing most of the work. Data center and AI segment revenue jumped 78% year over year to $7.3 billion in the third quarter, the segment's fastest growth in 15 years.

But that fourth-quarter forecast is a big drop from the third quarter, and PCs are the main reason. Intel expects PC unit sales industrywide to shrink around 12% this year. And it's planning for about another 10% decline in 2027. It doesn't expect PC sales to rebound for good until memory supplies improve and prices start to normalize.

What might Intel earn in 2030?

Intel's revenue may hit around $62 billion in 2026 if fourth-quarter sales land at the midpoint of its $15 billion to $16 billion forecast. This would be up about 17% over $52.9 billion in 2025.

Say revenue rises about 10% a year from there. This puts 2030 sales around $90 billion, over Intel's all-time high of $79 billion in 2021.

In the third quarter, Intel kept about 17 cents per revenue dollar as adjusted net income ($2.8 billion on $16.5 billion of revenue). I've assumed that grows to 20 cents by 2030. That's still under the more than 25 cents Intel kept in 2021. And it arguably leaves room for a foundry business that reported a $1.9 billion operating loss in the third quarter.

Investors buy both NVIDIA (NVDA) and Micron Technology (MU) to capture the spending on AI data centers: NVIDIA sells the computing systems, and Micron sells DRAM and NAND memory. Micron trades at 9.2 times earnings compared with 23.4 for NVIDIA, making it look like the cheaper way in. Yet NVIDIA said in August that soaring memory prices had prompted a reset of its gross margin expectations. So will memory prices keep rising, and can NVIDIA keep growing while it pays them?

Are Memory Prices Still Rising For Micron?

They are, although Micron expects the increases to slow. During its August 26, 2026 call, NVIDIA said memory price increases had exceeded its expectations and were headed even higher. For NVIDIA, that serves as a cost warning, but for Micron, those same prices are what it sells at.

Micron provided a pricing outlook on its September 30 call. Management guided fiscal Q1 2027 revenue of $60 billion to $63 billion, compared with $54.2 billion in fiscal Q4 2026. That forecast assumes only single-digit growth in the bits of DRAM and NAND that Micron ships, leaving price and product mix to supply the rest of the rise.

Management also said price increases would continue at a more moderate pace. Micron's 86.0% guide for its gross margin sits just below the 86.8% it reported for fiscal Q4.

Can NVIDIA Keep Growing As Memory Costs Rise?

So far it can, although its margin is slipping. NVIDIA guided fiscal Q3 2027 revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, compared with $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2. Management expects fiscal 2028 revenue to grow about 70% and said supply, including of its new Vera Rubin systems, would remain the bottleneck through at least the end of that year.

The memory bill shows up in the margin instead. NVIDIA reported a 75.0% gross margin for fiscal Q2 and guided 74% for fiscal Q3, plus or minus half a point. Management expects it to bottom at 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4, then settle at 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028 as NVIDIA's own price increases take effect.

NVIDIA's margins have also been far steadier than those of Micron. NVIDIA's operating margin averaged 61.7% over the last three twelve-month periods, compared with 35.3% for Micron. Over those periods, NVIDIA's twelve-month operating margin stayed between 58.1% and 65.2%, while Micron's twelve-month operating margin climbed from 5.2% to 74.6% in two years.

How Do NVIDIA And Micron Compare Head To Head?

Over the latest twelve months, Micron comes out ahead on growth and margin. Micron's revenue grew 256.3%, against 83.4% for NVIDIA. Its operating margin was 74.6%, compared with 65.2% for NVIDIA. Each company has debt under 1% of its market value.
